title: OS Structures & Kernel Design
summary: How a kernel is architected — monolithic, microkernel, hybrid — and the real performance-vs-isolation trade-off each design makes.

slides.markdown:
A kernel can put almost everything in one privileged space (**monolithic**), push almost everything out to user space (**microkernel**), or split the difference (**hybrid**). This isn't an academic taste question — it's a real trade-off between raw speed and fault isolation that shows up in why Linux, Minix, and Windows NT look so different underneath.

This topic gives you the vocabulary to place any OS on that spectrum and defend a trade-off, since "which is better" is a common interview trap with no single right answer.

slides.sectionTitle: Monolithic kernels: everything in kernel space
slides.markdown:
A **monolithic kernel** runs the scheduler, memory manager, filesystem, network stack, and device drivers all in kernel mode, in one address space, calling each other directly as ordinary function calls. Linux, the traditional Unix kernels, and Windows' core are all fundamentally monolithic.

The upside is speed: a filesystem call reaching a device driver is a plain function call within the same privilege level — no mode switch, no message passing, just a jump. The downside is blast radius: a bug in any one component (a buggy driver is the classic culprit) runs with full kernel privilege and can corrupt kernel memory or crash the entire machine.

This is precisely why a faulty third-party driver is historically one of the most common causes of a Windows blue screen or a Linux kernel panic — it's not sandboxed from the rest of the kernel at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Microkernels: minimal kernel, services in user space
slides.markdown:
A **microkernel** strips the privileged core down to the bare minimum — typically just scheduling, basic memory management, and inter-process communication (IPC) — and pushes filesystems, drivers, and network stacks out into ordinary user-space processes. Minix and QNX are canonical examples; seL4 is a modern, formally-verified microkernel used in safety-critical systems.

Because those services now run in user mode, a crashing filesystem driver is just a crashing process — the microkernel can restart it, and the rest of the system, including the kernel itself, stays up. The cost is that what used to be a direct function call (filesystem to disk driver) is now an IPC message that has to cross into the kernel and back out to another process — real, measurable overhead.

This trade is why microkernels are prized in safety-critical and high-assurance systems (seL4 is used in some avionics and defense contexts) where a single component's failure must never bring down the whole system.

The visual to take away: in the monolithic diagram, arrows inside kernel space are direct calls; in the microkernel diagram, every one of those same interactions has to cross a kernel/user boundary as an IPC message — twice as many boundary crossings for what used to be one function call.

slides.sectionTitle: Hybrid kernels: Windows NT, XNU — splitting the difference
slides.markdown:
A **hybrid kernel** keeps a microkernel-style architectural design — organized around distinct subsystems and message-passing conventions — but runs the performance-critical services in kernel space anyway, forgoing strict isolation for speed. Windows NT's kernel and Apple's XNU (used in macOS and iOS) are the standard examples.

XNU is a particularly clear case: it's literally built from the Mach microkernel plus large chunks of BSD Unix code, with much of that BSD code — networking, filesystems — running in kernel space rather than as separate user processes, sacrificing pure microkernel isolation for the performance of direct calls.

The honest framing: hybrid kernels are a pragmatic engineering compromise, not a theoretically pure third category — they borrow the structure of microkernels while making the same performance trade-off as monolithic ones for the pieces that matter most.

Every kernel design sits on the same axis: how much do you isolate components from each other, versus how fast can they talk?

| | Monolithic | Microkernel | Hybrid |
|---|---|---|---|
| Component communication | Direct function calls | IPC messages across kernel boundary | Mostly direct calls, some IPC-style structure |
| Fault isolation | Low — one bad driver can crash everything | High — a crashed service can often be restarted | Moderate |
| Typical overhead | Lowest | Highest (real IPC cost per crossing) | Low-to-moderate |
| Real examples | Linux, traditional Unix | Minix, QNX, seL4 | Windows NT, XNU (macOS/iOS) |

**How to decide which fits a scenario:** a general-purpose OS optimizing for throughput leans monolithic; a safety-critical system where one component's failure can't be allowed to cascade leans microkernel, accepting the IPC tax as the price of that guarantee.

slides.sectionTitle: Loadable kernel modules — monolithic flexibility without a rebuild
slides.markdown:
A pure monolithic kernel would need a full recompile and reboot to add support for new hardware — clearly impractical. **Loadable kernel modules (LKMs)**, like Linux's `.ko` files, solve this: they're kernel code compiled separately and inserted into the running kernel's address space at runtime (`insmod`/`modprobe`), immediately gaining full kernel privilege and calling kernel functions directly.

This gets monolithic kernels most of a microkernel's flexibility (add/remove drivers without rebuilding) while keeping monolithic performance (once loaded, it's just more kernel code, no IPC involved) — but it does **not** get microkernel-style isolation: a buggy module can still crash the whole kernel exactly like statically-compiled kernel code, since it runs with the same unrestricted privilege.

This is the mechanism behind `nvidia.ko`, filesystem drivers you install after the fact, and most third-party Linux kernel drivers.

Two research-driven designs push past the monolithic/microkernel spectrum entirely. An **exokernel** does almost nothing itself — it just securely multiplexes raw hardware resources and lets each application link in its own custom "library OS" implementing whatever abstractions it wants, trading a shared, general-purpose abstraction for application-specific ones tuned for performance.

A **unikernel** goes the opposite direction: it compiles a single application together with only the minimal OS code that application actually needs into one specialized, bootable image with no general-purpose kernel underneath at all — no unused drivers, no unrelated subsystems, sometimes no privilege separation within the image whatsoever.

Both are niche compared to Linux/Windows, but unikernels see real production use in specific high-density or security-sensitive serverless and edge-computing contexts, where a tiny, fast-booting, minimal-attack-surface image is worth the loss of general-purpose flexibility.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: assuming microkernels are always slower
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Microkernels are strictly worse in practice because IPC is always too slow."

**Why it's wrong:** this was a fair criticism of early 1980s-90s microkernel implementations (first-generation Mach, in particular) where IPC really was a severe bottleneck, and that reputation stuck. Modern microkernel designs — seL4 above all — have IPC paths measured in the low hundreds of cycles, engineered and formally verified specifically to close that historic gap, and seL4 is used today in real deployed systems (some automotive and defense platforms) precisely because its performance is acceptable for its guarantees.

**Correct model:** the performance gap is real but has narrowed dramatically with better IPC engineering, and it's a trade against a genuine, hard-to-get-elsewhere benefit — provable isolation — not a strictly dominated design. Whether it's "worth it" depends entirely on what a failure costs in your specific system.

slides.sectionTitle: Senior nuance: containers and userspace drivers as a partial microkernel retrofit
slides.markdown:
A staff-level observation: modern Linux systems have been retrofitting microkernel-style isolation onto a monolithic kernel piecemeal, without a full rewrite. **FUSE** (Filesystem in Userspace) lets a filesystem implementation run as an ordinary user process instead of kernel code — a bug there crashes that process, not the kernel — trading the monolithic filesystem's speed for isolation on a per-filesystem basis (this is exactly how `sshfs` and many modern filesystems avoid needing kernel patches at all).

Similarly, `io_uring` and userspace networking frameworks like DPDK move certain fast paths out of the traditional syscall-per-operation kernel model entirely, for different (performance) reasons than FUSE's isolation motive, showing the boundary between "what runs in the kernel" and "what doesn't" is still actively being redrawn today, not settled decades ago.

The interview payoff: recognizing that real systems mix strategies (mostly-monolithic Linux, with FUSE-style microkernel-ish escape hatches where isolation matters more than speed) is a stronger answer than treating the three categories as mutually exclusive whole-system choices.

slides.sectionTitle: How this shows up in production
slides.markdown:
When choosing infrastructure, this trade-off recurs outside OS kernels too. A monolithic application (all modules in one process, calling each other directly) is fast but one crashing module can take the whole process down — the same trade a monolithic kernel makes. Splitting into microservices communicating over the network is the same move a microkernel makes: better fault isolation, real per-call latency cost.

On Linux specifically, checking `lsmod` shows you which loadable kernel modules are active on a production box — a useful first step when diagnosing an unexplained kernel panic, since third-party modules (GPU drivers, some storage drivers) remain the most common source of monolithic-kernel-style total-system crashes.

Recognizing "this is the same isolation-vs-speed trade the kernel makes" is a transferable lens: it applies to service architecture, plugin systems, and browser extension sandboxing just as much as to kernel design.
